voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is the Son, one God with the Father and the Spirit, who died and was raised. We confessed him in the same Latin words the men we fought said, word for word, creed for creed. The quarrel was never about who he is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

What we had of him was books. Not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference. They reached us through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian — our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us.

None of us had known someone who saw him. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

glosses.plain_meaning: A martyr dies for the true faith. But our best-known dead were not killed by pagans. They were killed by imperial troops sent at the urging of a rival Christian party. That party has never once granted them the word. We do not accept its account of our own dead.
glosses.quick_meaning: Our dead, killed for the true faith -- and the word our rival will not grant them.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Wasn't every ancient church proud of its martyrs?' -- the difference here is who did the killing. These dead were killed by a Christian emperor's forces at a Christian rival's urging, and that rival called them not martyrs but merely dead men resisting correction. Commemorating them is therefore not general piety; it is the central argument, made at a graveside.
false_friend: a generic early-church martyr cult, killed by pagan Rome and admired by everyone since
'martyr complex' as a modern psychological label for self-dramatising suffering
relic veneration treated as superstition, rather than as the community's proof of its own claim
a settled category both sides recognise -- here the rival refuses the word outright

confidence.divergence_note: Doc_04 SS3.3 rates this the least Author-Gravity-encumbered material in the whole build: three distinct Donatist-voiced texts plus non-textual epigraphy, with no hostile literary mediation at any point in the epigraphic case. Two real limits are kept in view rather than smoothed. First, the commemorative sermon's date and authorship are Contested between two vendored authorities -- Mabillon's c. 340 against Monceaux's 12 March 317 with composition c. 320 and a hesitant attribution to Donatus the Great -- and neither is adopted (Doc_02 SS4, SS8). Second, the full Latin of the sermon and of the Passio Marculi has not been read beyond the passages checked, so this record runs through Monceaux's and Mabillon's analyses at those points rather than through the primary text directly.

confidence.divergence_note: The positive claim - that the confession on both sides of the African division was the same standard Latin Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy, and that the charge was schism and not heresy until Augustine's writing around 400 and the emperor's law of 405, a charge Augustine's own 417 report says they denied - rests on the whole shape of the polemical corpus rather than on one quotable creed of ours, because no creed of ours survives as a separate document. The three refusals in the second half are absences, not doctrines: no writing of ours argues substitutionary atonement, and the personal-Lord-and-Savior idiom postdates us by more than a millennium. Stated as absences so that a reader cannot mistake silence for denial.

confidence.divergence_note: The founding fact here - that the persecuting edict demanded the surrender of the scriptures, and that some African clergy complied - is Documented through the two inquiries preserved in Optatus's own appended dossier, and the surrender charge is argued in their own words by our own bishops as well as against them. But that dossier was selected and framed by a Catholic polemicist, and every narrative of the founding decade reaches us the same way. The Cyprianic descent is our own claim about ourselves and was contested by our opponents at the time; it is not an outside finding. And the last paragraph of the text field states an absence rather than a claim: no writing of ours arguing the resurrection survives, so nothing is asserted about how we argued it.

confidence.divergence_note: The positive claim - that the confession on both sides of the African division was the same standard Latin Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy, and that the charge was schism and not heresy until Augustine's writing around 400 and the emperor's law of 405, a charge Augustine's own 417 report says they denied - rests on the whole shape of the polemical corpus rather than on one quotable creed of ours, because no creed of ours survives as a separate document. The three refusals in the second half are absences, not doctrines: no writing of ours argues substitutionary atonement, and the personal-Lord-and-Savior idiom postdates us by more than a millennium. Stated as absences so that a reader cannot mistake silence for denial.

confidence.divergence_note: The founding fact here - that the persecuting edict demanded the surrender of the scriptures, and that some African clergy complied - is Documented through the two inquiries preserved in Optatus's own appended dossier, and the surrender charge is argued in their own words by our own bishops as well as against them. But that dossier was selected and framed by a Catholic polemicist, and every narrative of the founding decade reaches us the same way. The Cyprianic descent is our own claim about ourselves and was contested by our opponents at the time; it is not an outside finding. And the last paragraph of the text field states an absence rather than a claim: no writing of ours arguing the resurrection survives, so nothing is asserted about how we argued it.

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
He stood before the governor and was condemned, and was right. That is the Christ we kept nearest. When an imperial judge at Carthage courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days.

He died and was raised. His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. A bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them.

On how the cross saves, nobody among us wrote down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about whose hand may give what the church gives.

confidence.divergence_note: Assembled from a court transcript and from martyr texts, because those are the only places our own people speak at length about Christ - no christological or soteriological treatise of ours survives. The transcript is our own bishops' own words taken down by an imperial notary, which is unusually good ground; the printing it reaches this compilation through carries the worst OCR damage of any text in this corpus, so the wording is carried as reported sense and not as a quotable clause. That we confessed the same creed as our opponents is not our own claim but a finding all sides agree on: the division was called a schism, not a heresy, until Augustine's writing around 400 and the emperor's law of 405, and even then the charge rested on separation and not on any difference of creed.

confidence.divergence_note: Assembled from a court transcript and from martyr texts, because those are the only places our own people speak at length about Christ - no christological or soteriological treatise of ours survives. The transcript is our own bishops' own words taken down by an imperial notary, which is unusually good ground; the printing it reaches this compilation through carries the worst OCR damage of any text in this corpus, so the wording is carried as reported sense and not as a quotable clause. That we confessed the same creed as our opponents is not our own claim but a finding all sides agree on: the division was called a schism, not a heresy, until Augustine's writing around 400 and the emperor's law of 405, and even then the charge rested on separation and not on any difference of creed.

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
A traditor handed the scriptures over to be burned. When the persecutor came, some clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. We call such a man a traditor. His hand is no longer clean. He cannot ordain, baptize, or bless. What flows from that hand is nothing at all.

The word itself is Latin — tradere, to hand over. It names the act, not the motive. Whether a man gave up the books out of fear, or calculation, or simple weakness, we do not weigh. What we weigh is that he did it. And once he has, his hand cannot afterward give what the church gives.

This is not an old grudge over past cowardice. It is a claim about the sacrament. What we look for, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt.

citations.sentence: A traditor handed the scriptures over to be burned.

glosses.plain_meaning: When the persecutor came, some clergy handed the scriptures over to be burned. We call such a man a traditor. His hand is no longer clean. He cannot ordain, baptize, or bless. What flows from that hand is nothing at all.
glosses.quick_meaning: The one who handed over. A hand that failed then can give nothing now.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer asks, 'why not just forgive him and move on?' -- but forgiveness of the man was never the question here. The question was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give, and a whole century of baptisms and ordinations hangs on the answer. To waive the charge would concede that a sacrament is valid whatever the minister is, which is precisely the claim this communion was founded to refuse.
false_friend: traitor in the modern political sense -- a spy, a turncoat, a betrayer of a nation
an old grudge over past cowardice that reasonable people would have let go of
a procedural technicality about who signed what, rather than a claim about the sacrament itself
handing on the faith (the ordinary, positive sense of tradere) -- here the word names the opposite act

The doctrine's existence and centrality are Documented: Petilian of Constantina's own quoted proposition -- 'Conscientia namque dantis attenditur, quae abluat accipientis' -- was re-verified directly against the vendored npnf104 file (Doc_05 SS1, line 10280), and the Maximianist affair's own logic presupposes the doctrine as settled Donatist teaching rather than a hostile invention. results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
Because a hand that had given up the scriptures when the persecutor came could not afterward be trusted to give what it claimed to give. The Diocletianic persecution demanded that clergy hand over scripture and sacred vessels to be destroyed. Some carried the books out. Others refused and paid for it. We are the church that came out of that difference. The conviction was not reasoned from first principles. It was formed by what had actually happened: a man either carried the codices out or he did not, and that act decided whether his hand could be trusted later.

What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt. That is the whole of our doctrine in one sentence. The interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

And we held it because we had suffered for holding it. Persecution proved the conviction true. We were the pure, persecuted church, and what we would not concede was the proof.

confidence.divergence_note: Doc_04 SS3.1's own Confidence/Gravity Cross-Check splits this term in two and this record keeps the split. The doctrine's existence and centrality are Documented: Petilian of Constantina's own quoted proposition -- 'Conscientia namque dantis attenditur, quae abluat accipientis' -- was re-verified directly against the vendored npnf104 file (Doc_05 SS1, line 10280), and the Maximianist affair's own logic presupposes the doctrine as settled Donatist teaching rather than a hostile invention. The specific argumentative texture -- exactly how the Donatist side reasoned from traditio to invalid ordination to invalid sacrament -- survives substantially inside Augustine's refutation of it, and the Acta Purgationis Felicis reaches this record through Optatus's own selection and framing of his Appendix, court-acts character notwithstanding (Doc_02 SS1, Doc_03 Cluster 1).

confidence.divergence_note: The two internal quarrels named here - the Maximianist crisis and the silencing of Tyconius - are Documented, and both are among the best-attested things about us, for a reason that has to be stated: they are attested because an opponent found them useful. Augustine quotes the Bagai decree and reports Parmenian's letter because each proves a point against us. Our own account of either quarrel does not survive in any form. The treatment of conscientia as the word nearest what a modern speaker means by the heart is this compilation's own reading of how the word functions in Petilian's clause, offered as a reading and not as a term of art we defined.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
Tyconius lived it, and we silenced him for it. He was a layman of ours who argued from Scripture, at length and too well to be waved off, that the church is spread across the whole earth. If true, that meant we were the ones who had cut ourselves off from something real. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where it led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. He did not recant. He did not go over to the other side either. He kept saying it from inside, and we cut him off, and never took him back.

He wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us. He gathered almost no following among us. So there was room to keep arguing, and no room at all to be right.

We produced one man who could think, and we silenced him.

confidence.divergence_note: Documented for the man, the work, the rebuke and the fact of a subsequent condemnation. Two hedges are kept rather than smoothed. The mechanism of the condemnation - a conciliar sentence rather than some other exclusion - carries Augustine's own "perhibent," it is reported. And Tyconius's own formal standing within this communion is deliberately left open: he was tested against the bar for a distinct strand and rejected on the record, as a condemned individual voice with no attested following and no distinct communal practice, which is a different finding from settling what his membership status actually was.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
We are not four separate beliefs that happened to sit together. We are one thing, seen from four sides. A tainted hand gives nothing; so we are washed again, and that washing is our true entry, not a second attempt at something that already worked. We remember our own dead by name, at the grave, on the appointed day, because their death is the proof this conviction was never merely spoken. And we will not grant the emperor standing to decide which of two churches is the true one, because that is not his question to answer. Purity, the washing, the memory of our martyrs, and our refusal of the state — these are one conviction, not four.

And we will tell you plainly where holding it cost us something we did not resolve. The same rule we state absolutely did not, in fact, hold everywhere we state it. The same refusal we hold as principle we set aside three times when it served us. We say this ourselves, in the same breath as the conviction itself, because naming the strain is part of what we actually are.

From Petilian, one of our bishops at Constantina:

"What we look for is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt."

confidence.divergence_note: Documented, and unusually, through two structurally different channels rather than one. His letters survive only as quoted clause by clause inside the refutation written against them, where the selection effect is not incidental to the source but is the source. His interventions at the 411 Conference survive instead in a court transcript taken down by imperial notaries, where nothing was chosen by an adversary for refutation. Any claim about the fuller shape of his argument, beyond what the refutation preserves, is Inferential-Thin. Monceaux's dedicated chapter on him is vendored and remains unread.
